voice: lowercase-plain, honest about limits; proper nouns keep their casing

questions.q: what can it detect, and what can it not?
questions.a:
it detects known wifi and bluetooth signatures from some ALPR gear, Remote ID drones, body cams, separated trackers, and experimental recording-glasses signatures. switch on network cameras to flag nearby broadcasts from supported camera vendors. you can also star an exact device address to watch for it even without a known signature. starring a recognized device keeps its real category.

it cannot see wired, passive, cellular-only, or 5 GHz-only gear. wifi scanning is 2.4 GHz and moves between channels, so brief broadcasts can be missed. the beacon's dedicated bluetooth scanner listens continuously when enabled. a quiet screen means nothing recognizable announced itself in range, not that nothing is there.

questions.q: can i turn individual detectors on or off?
questions.a: yes. open Beacon, then detectors. each category changes what the beacon reports right away and stays set across restarts. flock/ALPR, drones, body cams, and glasses start on. trackers and network cameras start off because they can be noisy in ordinary places. scan radios is broader: it turns bluetooth or wifi listening off entirely.

questions.q: why do the Status count, radar dots, and category counts differ?
questions.a:
Status shows devices heard in roughly the last 45 seconds, excluding muted devices and offline replays. its total separates matched or watched devices from ambient Desert-mode broadcasts. a firmware category this app does not recognize is shown separately as unclassified, not assumed to be ordinary nearby gear. a star is included once in the total and does not replace a recognized device's category.

for readability, the radar draws at most 14 dots, with stars and recognized matches first. the dot cap does not limit the count, recording, or the Log. dots show signal strength, not direction or exact distance.

the strongest recent match card uses the device's name and last-heard age. if no match is present, it explicitly labels an unclassified or ambient fallback. switching a detector off keeps its recent count visible with an OFF label until those sightings age out. tap a nonzero category to see its Log; an empty disabled category opens its detector setting.

questions.q: where are everyday controls, and what do the Beacon status labels mean?
questions.a:
Beacon puts scan radios, detectors, and alerts near the top of its hardware controls. phone notifications, Live Mode, and display preferences have a separate phone group. per-category phone notifications are still independent of the board's buzzer or silent setting.

connecting, reconnecting, securing the link, and waiting for board status are different from an active scanning session. the radio summary reports unavailable status instead of assuming both radios are on. a bluetooth scanner fault can leave wifi scanning available; during firmware updates, detection may pause.

open the firmware summary for details. it distinguishes an available update, an update in progress, completion, failure, and a partly finished second-radio update. a current-catalog result only compares against the firmware information available to this app; it does not guarantee a newly published update has already been downloaded.

questions.q: how do i mute or ignore a device i already know about?
questions.a:
open the detection from the Log or map and tap mute. choose permanent, 1 hour, 24 hours, or at this place within 50 meters. earlier rows stay in the Log and show a muted label while the rule is active. app alerts and live views stay quiet for that device during the mute. muting removes its star; starring a muted device unmutes it. use select mode in the Log to mute several permanently. muted devices sit under managed devices on Beacon, where you can rename or unmute them.

permanent mutes are copied to the beacon, silence its hardware alerts, and still work with the phone away. timed and place mutes stay on the phone because the beacon has no clock or GPS to enforce their scope safely; they need the phone connected, and the beacon can still sound according to your alert setting. a mute follows the exact hardware address, so phones, tags, glasses, and other gear that rotate addresses may appear again under a new one. the list holds up to 256 devices.

questions.q: what does muting the beacon actually silence?
questions.a:
alerts under Beacon has three modes. buzzer plays category cues for eligible new hits; bursts can be combined and not every detection produces a sound. vibrate and silent both mute the board's detection sounds; vibrate gives phone haptics instead, subject to cooldowns. on Android they also defer to Do Not Disturb; on iPhone they play while the app is open, even during a Focus. this is the board's own voice, separate from muting one device you already know about. category phone notifications are independent opt-ins and can still arrive in silent mode; manage them under Beacon.

muting is not total, and the gaps are deliberate. a muted board also skips its startup jingle, because on an always-on unit a power cut and restore looks exactly like someone switching it on, and a muted board should not announce itself at 3am. two cues still play while muted: the shutdown motif, so you can hear it turn off instead of guessing, and the press-and-hold start beep on the button-equipped rev-B battery model, which only ever follows your own thumb. master volume at 0 is the one setting that silences all of it, which is why the volume slider stays live in all three modes. the LED keeps flashing at 0 unless you also switch on lights out.

the mute lives on the board, so a lost write could leave the two out of step. the app compares your mode against what the board reports on every status frame. if you asked for quiet and the board says it is audible, the app says it again straight away, then keeps saying it about every 30 seconds for as long as the two disagree. the other direction gives up on purpose: if you asked for sound and the board stays muted, the app stops claiming otherwise and shows silent for the rest of the session, without touching your saved setting.

trackers never beep on the board in any mode, and desert mode drops the board to silent while it runs. when you switch desert mode off yourself, your previous mode comes back, unless you picked a mode by hand while it was running, silent included. when the board ends desert mode on its own, after a factory reset, on an older board, or because another paired phone ended it, the app does not change your alert mode. if this phone saved a mode on the way into desert mode, it offers that one back instead. a restore alerts control appears on the desert card under Beacon, and under alerts as well when that section is shown. nothing changes until you tap it. the offer waits through app restarts. it moves to the top of the Beacon tab whenever board controls are unavailable, and onto the connect screen when the app is back to looking for a beacon, so it stays tappable with the beacon off or gone.

questions.q: what is Live Mode, and how do i put it on my lock screen?
questions.a:
Live Mode is the glanceable nearby counter. it shows detections heard in roughly the last 45 seconds, matching the Status screen, and keeps the phone connected to the beacon in the background. it is enabled by default after first setup and starts when a real beacon connection and the required phone permissions and system surfaces are ready. you can turn it off under Beacon. counts show on the lock screen by default; a switch under Beacon hides them, so the locked surface only says Live Mode is active. counts stay visible inside the app either way.

that switch reaches three surfaces on android: the locked Live Mode card drops to 'Live Mode active', a detection alert stops naming its category on the lock screen, and the android 16 status-bar chip drops its running count whether the phone is locked or not. on iphone it covers the lock screen card only, so the Dynamic Island and the Watch and CarPlay cells keep showing counts, and whether a detection alert shows its text on a locked screen is your own Show Previews setting.

on iphone it appears as a Live Activity on the lock screen and Dynamic Island, with compact system surfaces on supported Watch and CarPlay setups. on android it appears as an ongoing notification or Live Update. home-screen and compatible car widgets are separate: add the beacons widget from your system's widget picker (on android, Live Mode setup under Beacon can also add it for you). the widget counts a different thing on purpose: everything first heard today, resetting at local midnight, rather than the last 45 seconds. the icon row under that number only covers the categories that have an icon, so it can add up to less than the number above it, and offline-buffer replays count only when the beacon could date them to today; a replay whose time could not be reconstructed sits out of both. ios and android ultimately control whether these surfaces are allowed, so use the readiness checks under Beacon if one is missing.

after the first walkthrough, the app may ask for the phone permission Live Mode needs. choosing not now keeps detection and the Log working, but the lock-screen surface stays off until you finish setup under Beacon.

questions.q: can i flag one specific device to keep an eye on?
questions.a:
yes. open any detection and tap the star. to find something without a known signature, turn on desert mode, find it, star it, then turn desert mode off again. rename it under managed devices on Beacon so the Log reads like your Log. a recognized device keeps its actual category; the watchlist adds a watched-device match when no built-in signature matches. tracker-category detections never beep on the board, even when starred.

the Log and Map show a Watched category only when they contain matching detections. it includes currently starred devices in other categories and detections originally reported as watched. a saved star with no detected row does not create a pin or an empty category.

the watchlist lives on the beacon, survives reboots, and holds up to 256 devices. watching matches the exact hardware address, so it may not stick to phones, separated trackers, and other gear that rotate theirs. the app warns you when that is likely.

questions.q: what is desert mode, and when would i use it?
questions.a:
normally the beacon reports supported signatures and watched addresses. desert mode also reports ordinary nearby broadcasts, including phones, watches, earbuds, and TVs. it is useful for checking that scanning works, exploring sparse areas, and finding an unknown device to star or capture for a possible new signature. it is off by default and meant to be temporary.

a busy street can produce thousands of detections, so switch it off when you are done. it is not a complete inventory of every device: radio limits, address rotation, deduplication, and rate limits still apply. desert mode automatically silences the board while it runs. switching it off yourself restores your prior alert mode, unless you picked a mode by hand while desert mode was running, silent included. if the board ends desert mode on its own, your alert mode is left alone, and if this phone saved a mode on the way in, a restore alerts control appears on the desert card under Beacon, and under alerts as well when that section is shown, so the choice stays yours. the offer waits through app restarts. it moves to the top of the Beacon tab whenever board controls are unavailable, and onto the connect screen when the app is back to looking for a beacon, so it stays tappable with the beacon off or gone.

questions.q: does desert mode cap how much it logs?
questions.a:
the app retains a rolling window of up to 5,000 detections, in normal and desert mode. once that fills, older rows roll out and new detections keep arriving. export anything you need to keep before a long session. the limit bounds storage; it is not a promise that drawing thousands of map markers will stay fast on every phone.

the standard offline buffer records while the phone is away, skips desert mode's uncategorized nearby-device rows, and does not backfill rows that rolled out of the app's live Log. it is not an overflow archive.

questions.q: how do Log search, sorting, pause, and exports work?
questions.a:
search the Log by broadcast or custom name, vendor, or full or partial hardware address. combine search with a category and the all/new/offline filter, then sort by newest or strongest signal. strongest uses raw RSSI, not the confidence percentage.

pause freezes the displayed Log so you can inspect it; the app keeps receiving and recording detections. CSV and GPX exports use the matching rows and order from the Log you are viewing, including its paused snapshot. CSV can include rows without positions; GPX needs usable coordinates. resume first, then clear the search and category and choose All before exporting if you want all currently retained rows.

ordinary Log exports can contain your observation location and a drone's aircraft or operator coordinates. they do not use the location-removal switches from improve detection. review the file and destination before sharing.

questions.q: why does the Map show fewer detections, and how can i keep it responsive?
questions.a:
the Map defaults to Recent: devices with a known sighting in the last 15 minutes. open Map options and choose All history to include older or undated retained sightings. categories, mutes, and missing coordinates can also hide a pin. these are display rules, not a pause in recording or a deletion from the Log. opening an older detection in the Map switches to All history, but does not bypass a mute.

when the map is crowded or zoomed out, it groups nearby pins and can simplify marker symbols. zoom in for detail. the counts distinguish detections matching the current Map filters from retained located history and can flag a simplified view. clusters can mean fewer symbols than detections.

for a busy desert-mode session, use Recent, filter to the category you need, and switch off the community ALPR reference layer or map trails in Map options if you do not need them. turning off trail display does not stop breadcrumb collection. switch desert mode off when you finish looking for unknown devices.

questions.q: where is a tracker's breadcrumb trail, and does muting erase it?
questions.a:
open the tracker in the Log to see its breadcrumb trail on the detail map. the points are where your phone heard that same tracker address, not the tracker's own GPS route. the first point needs a fresh phone location. after that, another point is added only when at least 60 seconds have passed and the phone has moved at least 25 meters. the app keeps up to 120 points per tracker in memory for the current session; trails are not restored after restarting the app.

muting or ignoring that individual tracker stops new points while the mute is active and hides its pin from the main Map. it does not erase retained Log history or the existing session trail in Log details. unmuting lets new points resume; the muted interval is not filled in. silent alert mode and Focus or Do Not Disturb affect alerts, not breadcrumb collection.

the Seen with you panel summarizes observations from this session, not a stalking verdict. missing location, sparse sightings, or a rotating address can leave gaps or split one physical tag into separate detections.

questions.q: can i leave it recording without my phone?
questions.a:
yes, that is the offline buffer. it is off until you turn it on. once it is on, the beacon keeps logging detections while your phone is away, encrypted in its own flash and replayed when you reconnect with the matching phone key and sync completes. its storage is finite, so older records can eventually be overwritten. the Log's all/new/offline filter pulls up those buffered hits.

a transmitter that floods the air with fake camera or drone identities cannot overwrite the buffer in minutes. the beacon limits how fast it stores recognized detections: a burst of 256, then about one every 10 seconds, with the last few saved for devices it has kept hearing for at least 10 seconds. if that limit ever turns rows away, the Log and the offline buffer control under Beacon say DETECTION FLOOD REFUSED, because some real detections may be missing. the warning stays through restarts until the board buffer is erased.

be clear about what that encryption buys. your phone hands the beacon the key, and while the buffer is switched on the beacon keeps a copy of that key in flash so it can carry on recording across a reboot. anyone holding the board can therefore read what it stored: the buffer is not sealed against a seized beacon. switching the offline buffer off stops capture and erases the board's key, but does not erase the retained records. use the separate ERASE control under Beacon's offline buffer to delete those records; clearing the phone's Log is a different action. in standard mode, a buffer left uncollected through about six restarts is erased on its own.

if the app says BUFFER KEY NOT ACCEPTED, the existing history has been preserved but was not replayed. reconnect with the originating phone and its matching key, or explicitly erase the board buffer to transfer it after accepting that history will be lost.

the other honest limit is location. the beacon has no GPS of its own, so offline hits carry the last fix your phone shared before it left, and the beacon stops using that fix once it is about 18 hours old. hits it records after that still say what went by, with no position at all: no pin on the map, and empty location columns in an export. the fix lives in memory only, so a beacon that restarts while you are away has nothing to stamp until your phone comes back. and read those pins as where your phone last was, not where the beacon is. they are right while the beacon stays put; carry it around without your phone and they all sit at that one spot. a replayed hit either carries that fix together with how old it was, or reaches you with no position at all; the two never come apart.

questions.q: i can't find or pair my beacon. what should i try?
questions.a:
start with the simple checks. power the beacon with a known-good USB cable or switch it on, keep it within a few feet of your phone, make sure Bluetooth is on, and allow Nearby devices on android or Bluetooth on iphone. on older android phones, allow Location when asked because the operating system requires it for scanning. tap Scan for beacons, choose yours, then approve the phone's pairing request if it appears.

if the scan finds nothing, wait for the beacon to finish starting and scan again. if pairing does not finish, keep it powered and nearby, cancel, and retry. if another phone already uses the beacon, turn the beacon off and on, then connect the new phone within two minutes. if it still fails, email support@soyboi.tech.

questions.q: my other phone won't connect to the beacon
questions.a:
a beacon that already belongs to a phone accepts a new phone only during the first two minutes after a real power-up. turn it off and on, then connect within two minutes. the phone already paired to it can reconnect at any time, and a brand-new beacon is not affected.

this prevents someone nearby from pairing and reading where you have been. a firmware-update restart does not open the window.

questions.q: my beacon keeps restarting, or the startup sound plays over and over
questions.a:
it is usually the cable, not the beacon. the USB-C port is recessed, so a plug can feel seated while still falling short of full contact. push it straight in until it stops firmly.

if alerts are set to vibrate or silent, the board skips its startup jingle, so the same restart loop makes no sound at all. watch the LED instead, as long as lights out is off: it replays the startup flashes on every restart, and the slow idle heartbeat only settles in once the board stays up.

if that does not fix it, try a slimmer plug, a known-good cable, and a wall charger instead of a power bank. if it still restarts on a known-good cable and wall charger, email me and i'll sort it out.

questions.q: my AirTag is right next to me, why isn't the beacon flagging it?
questions.a:
first make sure trackers are enabled under Beacon; they start off. an AirTag near its owner's Apple gear can broadcast an owner-connected form that the beacon deliberately suppresses to reduce everyday noise. it needs to emit a supported separated broadcast before that signature can flag it.

for a test, leave the tag away from all of its owner's Apple devices, allow time for its broadcast state to change, then bring the beacon near it. do not treat fifteen minutes as a guaranteed timer. Tile and Samsung tags use different broadcasts and do not follow the same timing. a missing detection is not proof that no tracker is present.

questions.q: why did it take a while before a tracker on me showed up?
questions.a:
first check that trackers are enabled under Beacon; they start off. once a tag emits a supported separated broadcast, the beacon delivers sightings to the connected app from the first one it hears. the standard offline buffer waits through the first minute, so a briefly passing tag may reach the connected app but leave no buffered record.

tracker-category detections never beep on the board, even when starred. starring does not replace a recognized tracker with the watched category. phone notifications for trackers have their own switch under Beacon and start off. a notification is not an automated stalking alert.

tracker details can show when and where the same address was heard, subject to location and session limits. tags can rotate their addresses, so the same physical tag may later appear as a new detection.

questions.q: a tracker keeps coming back as a new device on the same trip. is that me or someone following me?
questions.a:
most often it is gear travelling with you. for AirTags and Google tags the beacon flags only the separated-from-owner broadcast, so a phone or earbuds still connected to their owner are skipped on purpose. Tile and Samsung tags have no such test and match on their finding broadcast alone, so one riding along with its own owner still shows up. an Apple device that goes offline sends the separated form too. that broadcast does carry a byte naming itself a tag or a phone, but it is self-declared and a tracker can set it to whatever it likes, so the beacon does not trust it and treats every separated broadcast the same.

the addresses then rotate, and that is what turns one thing into many rows. a separated tag holds its address for about a day, which is what makes starring or muting one stick. a device that is merely offline rotates far more often: on one of our own drives a single Apple device riding in the car arrived as ten different addresses in just under two and a half hours, handing off to a new address every fifteen minutes. a mute on the old address cannot hold against that.

read the pattern rather than any single row. something riding with you holds a steady strong signal for the whole trip and arrives as a chain of new addresses at a regular interval. something you passed shows up once or twice, weakly, and does not come back. the Seen with you panel summarizes the session; it is not a verdict, and a regular interval is not proof that something is yours.

trackers are opt-in and start off under Beacon. if you want a trip quiet, switching the category off is more reliable than muting addresses that are going to rotate away anyway.

questions.q: what does the match percentage mean, and why does a 'strong match' still say verify?
questions.a:
the percentage scores how specific the evidence was, not how likely it is that something is out there. under 50 reads 'weak match, verify' in amber, 50 to 79 is 'partial match', 80 and up is 'strong match'. the five-segment meter is the same number. it is not a probability, and it says nothing about how close the device is.

the small chip beside the verdict names what actually matched: a broadcast name, a manufacturer ID, a service UUID, a wifi network name, a Remote ID broadcast, or only the hardware address block. the strongest hits identify themselves, and a Remote ID drone broadcasts its own serial. a starred device matches every time because you starred that exact address, which is your own record rather than new evidence.

a hit can read 'strong match' and still be flagged, and the chip is why. an address-block match is amber whatever the percentage, because the block on its own leaves a real question open. 'OUI · VENDOR ONLY' means the block belongs to the maker, so it names Hikvision or Axon but not which of their products this is. 'OUI · CHIPSET ONLY' means it belongs to the radio chip inside, a part Flock shares with routers and home cameras, and the name and service IDs did not match at all. either way you get a confirm it checklist: look around, and check whether it is still there on a second pass.

whatever the number, a match means a radio that fits a known signature is switched on nearby. it does not mean a camera is recording, or that it is pointed at you.

questions.q: why doesn't the beacon pick up ALPR cameras very often?
questions.a:
often it will not, and that is the state of the gear rather than a fault with yours. the detector listens for Flock cameras broadcasting over bluetooth or 2.4 GHz wifi, and for Raven audio sensors over bluetooth only. many installs now stay silent either way, and the switch in Beacon settings says so next to it. a drive with no ALPR hits is a normal result.

what still fires is a device announcing something specific: a broadcast name, Flock's own hardware address block, or an external battery pack that names itself. those are real when they happen, but they are occasional rather than a steady stream, so treat a hit as something to confirm by eye and not as a count of the cameras you drove past.

this is why the map carries a community-mapped ALPR layer, on by default. those rings are mapped locations, not live detections, and they are the more reliable way to see where cameras have been recorded. the two layers do not confirm each other in either direction.

questions.q: the ALPR map shows a camera here, but the beacon isn't detecting it. is it broken?
questions.a:
no. hollow rings come from a separate community-mapped ALPR reference dataset. detection pins come from signals your beacon heard and may be recent or historical, depending on the map's history setting. neither layer confirms the other.

a camera may use cellular backhaul, be out of range, or emit no recognizable broadcast; the community record may also be incomplete or outdated. a detection near a ring, including an emphasized ring, is nearby observation evidence, not proof that the signal belongs to that exact mapped camera. a pin without a ring is not automatically a newly discovered camera either.

Map options controls the reference layer and additional mapped entries. attribution or tier labels describe the source record, not live detection confidence. if you know a device was broadcasting and it was missed, use improve detection to prepare a capture you can choose to share.

questions.q: what does a body camera detection actually mean?
questions.a:
it means a radio matching a known body cam signature is switched on nearby. it does not mean a camera is recording. the broadcast carries no recording state at all, so the beacon cannot tell a rolling camera from one sitting in its mount. a hit tells you the gear is present and powered, nothing more. the detector was validated against body cams worn by officers on normal patrol.

four signatures land under this one label and they are not equally strong, so the detection names which one fired. 'BWC DEVICE' is the tag Axon body cams broadcast about themselves; it rides in the advertisement rather than the address, so it holds even when the device randomizes its address, and it is the strongest one the beacon carries. 'Axon OUI' is Axon's own address block without that tag, so it is Axon-made gear of some kind, and they ship docks and other products on the same block. 'Utility BodyWorn' matched either the broadcast name, which is a deliberate self-identification, or the address block alone, which is weaker. 'Motorola Solutions OUI' is a vendor proxy rather than a camera signature: the block is theirs, and so are their two-way radios, docks, and site equipment.

read the signature line rather than the category word. the Motorola proxy is a switch of its own nested under body cams in Beacon settings, and it is off by default: at one airport capture every single one of its 27 hits turned out not to be a body camera, so it is opt-in rather than on.

questions.q: a drone kept showing up after it landed or was switched off. is that real?
questions.a:
it can be. Remote ID comes from the aircraft itself, not its controller or your phone. in the US the FAA requires the broadcast from takeoff to shutdown, not just until landing, so a drone left powered on the ground can keep broadcasting. the aircraft has its own battery and power button, so closing the app or switching off the controller does not turn it off, and on DJI drones a single press can leave it running because powering down takes a short press and then a press and hold. rules differ outside the US.

open the detection and expand Technical details. the Status row, if there is one, reads 'On ground', 'Airborne', 'Emergency', or 'System fault', the last meaning its Remote ID system has failed. that is the drone's own claim, and the beacon only updates it when the drone sends a position. 'On ground' on a detection that is still updating means a powered aircraft that is still transmitting. 'Airborne' means it says it is flying, which a drone can do on its own after losing its controller. a missing row proves nothing.

none of this says whether its camera is recording. Remote ID carries no recording state, and a powered drone on the ground can still film.

to check whether it is still live, watch the Status screen, which drops a device about 45 seconds after it was last heard. the Map's Recent view keeps a pin for about 15 minutes at its last position, so a pin that stays put is not proof it is still broadcasting.

a Detail ending in 'gear, no Remote ID' is a different kind of hit. only a drone maker's address block matched, which that maker's controllers and other gear can share, so there is no Status row or aircraft position. that fallback is off by default, and desert mode turns it on.

questions.q: can it find a hidden camera in an airbnb or hotel room?
questions.a:
sometimes. turn on network cameras and the beacon flags nearby wifi broadcasts whose hardware addresses belong to supported camera vendors. a hit names the vendor, not the device, so it could be a doorbell, recorder, disclosed camera, or another product from the same maker.

it cannot detect wired, analog, cellular-only, powered-off, motion-idle, 5 GHz-only, or unknown cameras that do not emit a recognizable signal. it does no lens or infrared detection. an empty scan does not mean the room is clean. use it alongside a physical sweep: check smoke detectors, vents, and mirrors, look for lens glints with a flashlight, and check for infrared lights through your phone camera in the dark.

questions.q: how far away can it hear something?
questions.a:
usually tens of meters, not whole neighborhoods. with clear outdoor line of sight, a pole-mounted device may reach toward 100 meters. walls, vehicles, clothing, and bags can cut that to only a few meters. wifi often carries farther than bluetooth, and a real antenna on a pole carries farther than a body cam under a jacket.

placement matters too: the beacon hears more on a dashboard than inside a backpack. treat it as 'what is around me right now.' a quiet screen means nothing recognizable announced itself in range, not that nothing is there.

questions.q: what does the signal number mean, and why is a weak signal not the same as far away?
questions.a:
the number in a detection's SIGNAL panel is RSSI, in dBm. it is how loud that radio sounded to the beacon at that moment. it is always negative, and closer to zero is stronger, so -45 is much louder than -90. the graph below it is the same number over time, so it climbs as you close in and drops as you move away.

RSSI is not distance. every radio picks its own transmit power, and that choice moves the number far more than walking does. a pole-mounted camera or a drone on wifi transmits hard and can read strong from across a street. smart glasses and a tracking tag whisper on bluetooth to save battery, so they can be a few meters away and still read weak. a body cam under a jacket loses more on top of that.

so compare a device to itself, not to other devices. watch whether one device's own line climbs as you move. between two different devices, the stronger number does not mean the closer one. the Log's strongest sort and the map pin both use raw RSSI, so they rank loudness, not nearness.

questions.q: how long does the battery last?
questions.a: roughly 4 to 7 hours of continuous scanning on a charge, depending on how much is around to detect: about 4 hours in a device-dense crowd and up to 7 somewhere quiet. eco mode stretches it by easing off the wifi sweeps while bluetooth keeps running full-time. the slim model has no battery and scans while suitable USB power is available; a power bank lasts only as long as its capacity allows.

questions.q: why does the battery percentage jump around?
questions.a:
the battery version estimates charge from voltage instead of using a dedicated fuel-gauge chip. the radios draw power in bursts, so heavy scanning can make the voltage dip and the percentage fall a few points, then rise again when the load eases. lithium voltage also stays fairly flat through the middle of a charge, so the estimate moves faster near full and empty.

the firmware smooths the reading, but a few percent of drift is normal. read it as a fuel gauge, not a stopwatch: full, half, and getting low are what it does well.

questions.q: where does my data go?
questions.a:
detections are retained on your phone, and the optional offline buffer stores records on the beacon while your phone is away. neither is automatically uploaded. the app's automatic network requests are for map tiles, firmware checks and downloads, and the community ALPR dataset. that reference layer is on by default and can be switched off in Map options.

update and dataset downloads attach no location, map view, or detection data, though the host sees the ordinary request and your IP address. map tile requests reveal the area you are viewing to the tile provider, but do not include detections. exports and improve detection reports leave only when you choose to share them. opening bundled Help itself makes no network request; external help links open the browser.

questions.q: does the app need access to my files or storage?
questions.a:
no broad storage permission is needed. Log exports and improve detection reports are files the app writes in its own private space. when you share one, the system sharing or mail flow opens and you choose where it goes. nothing is uploaded automatically.

the app's own copy of each export is temporary. once a copy is more than an hour old, the app deletes it the next time it starts (on android, also the next time you export). clearing the Log deletes all of those copies straight away, so if an export is evidence, save or send it somewhere outside the app first. a copy you saved or sent elsewhere is not touched.

clearing the Log also removes the app's detection notifications. on android it deletes the cached map tiles too, because they record the areas you viewed; android keeps those tiles only in the app's private internal storage, up to about 100 MB. on iphone the map is Apple Maps, which manages its own cache, so the app has no tile cache to clear. clearing the Log does not erase the board's offline buffer; that has its own ERASE control under Beacon.

if you attach a photo to an improve detection report, you choose that photo through the system picker; this does not grant access to your whole photo library. the app re-encodes the selected image to remove embedded metadata before attaching it. anything visible in the image can still identify a person or place, so review it too.

questions.q: why does the app want my location?
questions.a:
location adds observation pins, tracker breadcrumbs, and place mutes within 50 meters. iPhone also needs it for Live Mode's background operation. Android 8 through 11 requires Location for bluetooth scanning itself; newer Android versions use Nearby devices permission for the connection. Android Live Mode does not request background Location.

your phone sends its current fix over encrypted bluetooth to your own beacon. if the phone leaves, buffered non-drone hits may use that last fix until it is about 18 hours old. a board restart forgets the fix. those locations describe where the phone last was, not later movement of the board.

ordinary Log exports can contain observation, aircraft, and operator coordinates and have no location-removal switches. improve detection has separate switches: your observation and the operator location start off, while aircraft location starts on. opening a map also requests tiles from Apple Maps on iOS or OpenStreetMap on Android, revealing your viewed area and IP address, but not detections. on iPhone and newer Android versions you can decline Location and still detect and keep a Log; location-dependent features will be limited.

questions.q: does a pin show where the camera is, or where i was?
questions.a:
for most detections, the pin uses the strongest signal sample that also had a usable observation location. a stronger located RSSI sample moves the pin; an equal or weaker one leaves it in place. a strong signal without a location cannot locate the device. this estimates where you heard it best, not where the device is: read it as 'this was in range around here.'

tracker details can also show a session breadcrumb trail of your observation positions. offline records may instead use the last fix your phone shared before leaving; that does not track a beacon carried without the phone.

Remote ID drones are the exception when they broadcast valid aircraft or operator coordinates. those positions come from the broadcast. a vendor-only drone match does not provide aircraft GPS just because it is in the drone category.

questions.q: do i need an account or a subscription?
questions.a: no. no account, no cloud, no fees, no telemetry. buy the beacon once, use the free app forever.

questions.q: what happens if soyboi disappears tomorrow?
questions.a: local scanning and your saved Log do not need an account or a project server. the app and ESP32-S3 firmware source are published on GitHub, so others can maintain them. new hosted firmware downloads and community-map dataset refreshes could stop if their hosting disappears; map tiles also depend on their providers. the hardware can still detect using its installed signatures.

questions.q: does it get better over time?
questions.a:
detection improves through firmware and app updates, not automatic learning on the board. the app checks for compatible firmware and offers an update you choose to install over bluetooth; supported beacon updates can include both radios. the web flasher is another option over USB. app features and bundled FAQ changes arrive through app releases.

to help with a missed device, use improve detection under Beacon to capture observations, review the location choices and optional photo, then choose Review & Share. you still confirm the destination and send it in your mail or sharing app. no report is sent automatically.

questions.q: is the hardware open source too?
questions.a: the app and the ESP32-S3 firmware are fully open source, and always will be. the nRF scanner firmware and the board design itself are not published. you buy the hardware, you own every byte it produces.
